Pourquoi voter au fédéral quand on se se: Why vote federally when you feel excluded?
À quelques jours des élections, une ques: Just days before the election, one question haunts the streets of Montréal-Nord, Saint-Michel and Côte-des-Neiges: why vote federally?
Nous ne sommes plus qu’à trois jours du: We’re only three days away from the vote, and I think the subject of our article comes at the right time: what’s the point of voting federally?
À La Converse, au fil de nos reportages,: At La Converse, over the course of our reporting, we’ve noticed a recurring phenomenon: the three levels of government are often confused, and the federal government seems, we’re told, so far removed from citizens that they have a hard time taking an interest in it. All the more so since, during this election campaign, international issues have dominated the debate: the trade war with the United States, who would be the best leader to face Donald Trump, and so on. But which candidate has actually talked about safety in so-called disadvantaged neighbourhoods, and about gun violence?
Pour cet article, nous avons rencontré u: For this article, we met with a city councillor who mobilizes citizens to go vote, as well as federal candidates from the ridings of Bourassa and Saint-Léonard–Saint-Michel, who explained to us why voting federally matters.
Je dois préciser que mon sujet a changé: I should point out that my story changed shape several times. At first, I wanted to profile organizations that advocate for citizens to take part in the electoral process, but several of them don’t serve our community, and the others weren’t available. It’s a very busy time, after all!
Et puis, quand il s’agit de rencontrer d: And when it comes to meeting candidates, the closer election day gets, the less available they are… In the end, I was able to interview one candidate from the Liberal Party and one from the New Democratic Party.
À la fin de l’article, je donne quelques: At the end of the article, I share a few resources to help you better follow the voting process.
<strong><em>À quelques jours des électio: Just days before the election, one question haunts the streets of Montréal-Nord, Saint-Michel and Côte-des-Neiges: why vote federally if nothing changes in my neighbourhood? In these neighbourhoods, often grappling with precarity, insecurity and a sense of abandonment, voter fatigue is palpable. For many, voting isn’t the promise of a better future, but simply a duty, something done on principle. Behind this fatigue, confusion over the different responsibilities of each level of government muddies the waters and deepens disengagement. And yet, voices are rising, well known in their neighbourhoods. Municipal officials, researchers and ordinary engaged citizens are working hard to rebuild the ties between politics and the people. Our report.
Jeudi 10 avril. <l1>Après un vox pop réa: Thursday, April 10. <l1>After a vox pop at the Pretty Little Thing nail salon</l1>, we stop a passerby in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood. Though visibly in a hurry, she pauses and takes the time to share her concerns ahead of the federal election. “What bothers me is the bike lanes! Here in Saint-Michel, everything is far away, and yet they want to stop us from using our cars. Public transit isn’t always the best solution.” Two weeks before the election, it isn’t the first time we’ve heard this comment, which reveals the confusion between municipal, provincial and federal responsibilities. We explain to her that bike lanes are the City’s responsibility, not Ottawa’s. Her gaze drifts off into space: “Oh… Really? Well, I don’t know who I’m voting for yet, but I’m going to vote.”
Cet échange en dit long sur le sentiment: This exchange speaks volumes about the sense of distance from federal politics felt by many voters in Montréal’s more outlying neighbourhoods.
<strong>« Il y a beaucoup de confusion e: “There’s a lot of confusion between the roles of the municipal, provincial and federal governments”
Stéphanie Valenzuela, conseillère munici: Stéphanie Valenzuela, city councillor for the borough of Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce in Montréal, understands well the sense of distance many voters feel toward the federal government. For several weeks now, she has been criss-crossing the streets of her district, knocking on doors and encouraging citizens to exercise their right to vote – an effort she carries out on a non-partisan basis. We reach her by videoconference on the day advance polls open.
« Les citoyens ne sont pas désintéressés: “Citizens aren’t uninterested, they’re disoriented,” she begins. “There’s a lot of confusion between the roles of the municipal, provincial and federal governments.” Confusion that, in her view, undermines civic engagement.
Dans un quartier comme Côte-des-Neiges,: In a neighbourhood like Côte-des-Neiges, where most residents come from immigrant backgrounds, this confusion often translates into a lack of bearings, she continues. “People contact me about issues that aren’t within my jurisdiction. Often, it’s just that they don’t have a point of contact, they don’t know where to look.”
Elle devient alors ce point de départ. «: So she becomes that starting point. “Even if it’s a question about immigration or health issues – which aren’t municipal matters – I take the time to listen to them, guide them and point them to the right resource.” It’s through these small gestures, she says, that bonds of trust are built.
« Quand une personne comprend que tu l’a: “When someone realizes you helped them once, they come back. And sometimes, they send you their neighbour, their cousin, their mother… That’s how you build a support network in the neighbourhood, and how you manage to better meet people’s needs.”
Le palier fédéral, poursuit-elle, est so: The federal level, she continues, is often seen as the one furthest removed from citizens. Yet without it, many projects would struggle to get off the ground, since municipal and provincial governments frequently depend on its support.
Elle prend l’exemple du quartier Namur–H: She gives the example of the Namur–Hippodrome neighbourhood, a vast urban redevelopment project in her borough. “It’s a project that perfectly illustrates the complexity of shared jurisdictions. The federal government funds the construction of social and affordable housing; the province redistributes the funds; and the City plans the land. But the concrete results are slow in coming.”

Et puis, il y a les délais, les lourdeur: And then there are the delays, the red tape, the decision-making channels that don’t communicate with one another. Ms<sup>. </sup>Valenzuela explains: “In Quebec, it’s even more complicated. Unlike in other provinces, the federal government can’t fund municipalities directly. The money goes through the province, which then decides how to allocate it. So it takes time. And when people don’t see results, they tune out.”
Ce sentiment d’impuissance, elle le cons: She sees this sense of powerlessness every day on the ground. “People tell me, ‘We vote, but nothing changes,’ but I insist on making people understand that not voting isn’t a solution. If you don’t vote, someone else will decide for you. And that person might not have the same priorities as you,” she says with a shrug.
Ses convictions poussent parfois la cons: Her convictions sometimes push the city councillor beyond her formal role as an elected official. “It’s not officially part of my duties, but I’ve accompanied residents to the federal polling station. Because they didn’t know how to get there. Because they weren’t sure what to bring. Because they needed support through the process,” she says.
« Ce n’est pas normal que les gens soien: “It’s not normal for people to be this lost. We have to give them the keys, explain the issues to them, make the information digestible. Not everyone has the time or the ability to read party platforms or watch debates. You can’t demand that level of engagement when living conditions themselves make it difficult,” the city councillor concludes.
<strong>« La norme du citoyen à laquelle: “The standard citizen that all political discourse is aimed at is the white middle class”
Céline Bellot, professeure à l’École de: Céline Bellot, a professor at the Université de Montréal’s École de travail social, argues for her part that the supposed lack of interest among people from working-class backgrounds or marginalized groups is “a myth that it’s time to deconstruct.”
Elle ne remet pas en cause l’engagement: She doesn’t question these people’s political engagement, but rather points to the systemic barriers that hold back their participation.
Elle dénonce un système électoral pensé: She denounces an electoral system designed for an “average” voter who is far from representative of Canada’s diversity. “The standard citizen that all political discourse is aimed at is the white middle class. Even if it isn’t said explicitly, that’s what the platforms are built on. They’re speaking to a white majority,” she states bluntly.
Dans ce contexte, les populations racisé: In this context, racialized and Indigenous people, as well as those experiencing homelessness or living with disabilities, are excluded from a political narrative that doesn’t recognize them. “As soon as you step outside the framework of the average citizen – someone with a fixed address, a means of transportation and an ‘acceptable’ interest in politics – you face barriers to access. And sometimes, a form of disengagement, but one that is mostly a reaction to exclusion.”
Ce phénomène se vérifie également dans l: This phenomenon also holds true in Indigenous communities, with which Ms<sup>. </sup>Bellot works closely. “We see a real gap between participating in a federal system and demands for autonomy or self-determination,” she explains. “Clearly, it clashes. It’s not disengagement, it’s a clear demand: this isn’t the framework in which these communities want to engage politically.”
M<sup>me </sup>Bellot insiste : il faut: Ms<sup>. </sup>Bellot insists: we need to stop believing that voting is the only valid expression of political engagement. “You can have all kinds of actions [volunteering, protests, collectives, civic engagement] and political engagement that won’t be considered political engagement, because you’re not in the traditional parties, because you’re not a youth member of a political movement. What’s expected is that everyone plays the same game, but the rules of that game aren’t the same for everyone.”
Et même dans les rares cas où les partis: And even in the rare cases where political parties address minority groups – in certain ridings where these groups become electorally significant – it remains a one-off, circumstantial strategy. “The dominant political discourse is still aimed at a middle-class Canadian or Quebecer who isn’t part of a minority,” she stresses.
Selon la chercheuse, les discours politi: According to the researcher, political discourse is indeed aimed at the middle class. “It’s invoked, for example, to say taxes will be cut, and almost all political promises are directed at that group – without anyone really knowing very clearly what the ‘middle class’ even is, by the way,” she remarks.
« Et pourquoi blanche ? reprend-elle. Pa: “And why white?” she continues. “Because there’s very little discourse on issues of racism, on issues of racial discrimination. It’s generally not part of the promises. It’s simply because they’re not addressing a population that has those difficulties or those problems.”
Et en cette période électorale où les qu: And in this election period, when immigration issues long dominated the debates, the expert is concerned about another phenomenon: “I’m not convinced that immigrants, even once they’ve become citizens, want to take part in this political game. Not in this context, not with this discourse that links immigration to all kinds of structural failures, notably the housing crisis, the crisis in public services, etc.”
<strong>Abdelhaq Sari</strong> <strong>–: Abdelhaq Sari – “What makes the difference is when people really know you. Not just during a campaign.”
Sur le terrain, on sent parfois cette te: On the ground, you can sometimes sense this tension between the exclusion some citizens feel and the candidates’ desire to act.
<strong>Montréal-Nord</strong>. Rendez-v: Montréal-Nord. We’ve arranged to meet in front of the campaign office of Abdelhaq Sari, Liberal candidate in the riding of Bourassa. The space is bright, the picture window covered with posters bearing his photo. The campaign manager welcomes us while two volunteers in their sixties, both on the phone, provide information to voters. One, of North African origin, wears a hijab. The other, a white woman, speaks in hesitant Spanish: “Sí, pueden votar ya, del 18 al 21,” while her colleague follows almost like an echo: “Yes, you can already vote in advance starting today.”
Le candidat est absent pour le moment, n: The candidate isn’t here at the moment, we’re told. He went to drop by a polling station, but he shouldn’t be long. About fifteen minutes later, a voice calls out: “Ah, the boss is here!” Through the picture window, we spot him: brown suit, broad smile and an almost presidential wave to a car honking as it drives by. Abdelhaq Sari walks into the office.
En ce premier jour de vote par anticipat: On this first day of advance voting, he is visibly pleased. “This morning, I got a lot of calls from people who went to vote. They waited 40 minutes, sometimes an hour. There were really a lot of people!” The turnout motivates him: “It doesn’t slow us down. We keep calling, keep mobilizing.”
Conseiller municipal à Montréal-Nord dep: A city councillor in Montréal-Nord for eight years, the Liberal candidate says he wants to extend his influence to the federal level. “I have people’s trust, I have experience and I want to defend their interests in Ottawa. The issues are there: housing, immigration, the cost of living.”
Mais il ne se fait pas d’illusions : con: But he has no illusions: convincing people remains a challenge. Some tell him voting is pointless or that politicians are all corrupt… “If you believe nothing changes, then stay out of the process. But afterwards, don’t come asking elected officials to account for themselves,” he says sharply. He pauses. “The truth is, if you don’t take part in this process, you can’t hope to influence politics. Protests don’t accomplish much, in my opinion. On the other hand, people working inside the system – that really has an impact on the things you care about,” he asserts.
Le candidat parle lui aussi d’une certai: The candidate also speaks of a certain confusion among voters: “A lot of people can’t tell the difference between levels of government. Who does what? It’s fuzzy.” For him, the answer lies in civic education and consistency: “What makes the difference is when people really know you. Not just during a campaign. When you’ve been there for them, they remember.”
Il évoque des conférences données dans l: He mentions talks he’s given at community centres and his conversations with young people about violence and crime. For him, it’s these concrete gestures, far from the spotlight, that build trust. And that trust, he says, is all the stronger in a riding like Bourassa, where voters can see themselves in him. “Yes, I’m an elected official, but above all, I’m someone from their community, I’m North African. Someone who feels what they feel. That makes the difference.”
Selon lui, les citoyens de sa circonscri: According to him, citizens in his riding are concerned about international conflicts: the situation in Gaza, the war in Ukraine, tensions in Lebanon, the strife in Sudan. “People are asking, ‘What’s my representative’s position? The party’s? The government’s?’ We have to give them clear answers.” He notes that a motion on the situation in Gaza, which he presented to city council, was adopted unanimously. “We wanted to send a message of dialogue and respect between communities.”
Il doit filer : un autre événement de ca: He has to run: another campaign event awaits him five minutes from the office. We go with him.
Sur place, il est vite entouré de visage: Once there, he’s quickly surrounded by familiar faces. A family of Moroccan origin approaches him, visibly happy to run into him. “We took the opportunity to come vote today, since it’s a day off!” the father says.
L’un de ses enfants n’est pas en âge de: One of his children isn’t old enough to vote, but his father wanted him to witness the moment. “He was playing video games; I told him, ‘Come on, let’s go!’”
Il poursuit fièrement : « Depuis qu’on a: He continues proudly: “Ever since we’ve had the right to vote in Canada, we’ve done it. It’s a duty to choose who will represent us.” To back up his commitment, he even served as a volunteer driver during Abdelhaq Sari’s nomination race, shuttling neighbours between their homes and the polling stations. “Mr. Sari doesn’t even know,” he lets slip with a burst of laughter. “I do it because he’s always been there for us. He’s not just a name on a poster. He’s someone we know, for real.”
<strong>Marwan El Attar : « Il faut bras: Marwan El Attar: “We’ve got to rattle the cage!”
<strong>Mercredi 23 avril.</strong> C’es: Wednesday, April 23. It’s in a small Italian café in Saint-Michel, late in the afternoon, that Marwan El Attar – federal candidate for the New Democratic Party (NDP) – arranges to meet us. Sharp-eyed, he sits down, coffee in hand. At 32, the lawyer has put his career on hold to avoid any conflict of interest. “I got the nomination two days before the campaign started. I’ve been running ever since!” And it’s not a metaphor. Since the announcement, he’s been going from meeting to visit to conversation, non-stop.
Marwan El Attar est né et a grandi à Sai: Marwan El Attar was born and raised in Saint-Léonard, brought up by a single mother along with his two brothers. He doesn’t come from a privileged background. “I grew up in precarity. I understand the neighbourhood’s issues because I lived them.” It’s this direct connection to the community that, in his view, makes all the difference.
« Je suis un homme racisé, du quartier,: “I’m a racialized man, from the neighbourhood, young. That reassures [voters]. They see that I understand what they’re going through.”
Pourquoi se lancer maintenant ? « Rien n: Why run now? “Nothing’s moving. We’ve got to rattle the cage!” He speaks frankly about the old housing, the inadequate transit, the inflation squeezing families. “They always promise something will be done. But nothing happens. They take us for granted.”
Dans ce quartier, l’abstention atteint p: In this neighbourhood, abstention reaches nearly 43%. He attributes this rate to residents being unable to think long-term: “When you live in a disadvantaged neighbourhood, you think about surviving first. Not about thriving. You forget that you can change things.” So he’s betting everything on being close to people.
Avec une poignée de bénévoles, Marwan si: With a handful of volunteers, Marwan makes the rounds of the places where people live their lives. That evening, there’s no big door-to-door operation. Just a few steps down the street, flyers in hand. He spots a passerby, approaches and strikes up a conversation. The man seems uncomfortable, nods politely, then walks away. Another, barely addressed, raises his hand in a curt gesture, clearly signalling he’s not interested.
Marwan ne se démonte pas. « Parfois, c’e: Marwan isn’t fazed. “Sometimes, that’s how it goes. But other times, it opens a door. All it takes is one conversation. One familiar face.”
Il sait que chaque interaction, même brè: He knows every interaction, however brief, can plant a seed of doubt, a desire to learn more, maybe even to vote. He sees himself as a bridge between politics and citizens who are often forgotten. “I live with my wife. And I ask myself, ‘If we had kids tomorrow, what kind of society would they grow up in?’ Groceries are already tough. We can’t even afford to buy a house.” Even though he works as a lawyer, Marwan feels the economic pressure too.
Et même si les passants rencontrés ne so: And even though not every passerby is receptive, he keeps going, a stack of flyers in hand, rattling the cage, slowly but surely.
